html:
An Ob-Ugric people of the middle and lower Ob River in western Siberia, shown on the map in 1530. With their neighbours the Mansi they speak the languages closest to Hungarian.

The Khanty lived by fishing, hunting, trapping fur animals and, in the north, herding reindeer. They were organised in small princedoms with fortified towns, and medieval Russians knew their land as Yugra, a source of sable and other furs. Traders and raiders from Novgorod took tribute there from the late 11th century.

In 1530 many Khanty paid tribute to the Tatar Khanate of Sibir. After Yermak broke Sibir in the 1580s, Russian forts went up along the Ob, and the Khanty became subjects of the tsar during the Russian conquest of Siberia. Orthodox missions in the 18th century tried to end their bear ceremonies and shamans, with limited success. Today they share the Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug, which is also Russia's main oil region.
